title: Currencies: A weak $A threatens RBA's inflation fight
full_text:
The Australian dollar has come under renewed selling pressure, further complicating the Reserve Bank of Australia's effort to get inflation back under control, which has already pushed borrowing costs to the highest in 18 years.
The Aussie hit a fresh seven-month low overnight after a senior US Federal Reserve official warned that a supersized half of one percentage point interest rate increase may be on the table next month should inflation in America remain too high.
A few hours later, US consumer price data came in hotter than expected, sending the greenback and bond yields surging and the Australian dollar tumbling as bond traders rapidly repriced their rate expectations.
On Wednesday, the Aussie was trading around US68.78¢, having tumbled to as low as US68.42¢ in New York trading.
"It certainly pushes the RBA in a certain direction, which is to hike," said Commonwealth Bank head of foreign exchange and international economics Joseph Capurso, referring to the depreciation in the currency. "A weaker Aussie does not help the RBA because of higher imported inflation. But I probably wouldn't say it will force the RBA to hike ... but it's certainly uncomfortable."
RBA governor Michele Bullock has recently emphasised how higher interest rates strengthen the Australian dollar, which then lowers the cost of imported goods. But renewed strength in the US dollar could undermine that disinflationary effect.
Bond markets are still pricing in a higher chance of a rate rise in Australia than a cut, with traders pricing in a one in four chance of a sixth consecutive increase by early next year. That would take the cash rate above 5 per cent, the highest since the global financial crisis.
While in the US, markets are now fully priced for the Fed to raise interest rates next month by a quarter of one percentage point, but have also started to weigh the possibility of a jumbo move.
Fed governor Christopher Waller warned overnight that if core inflation, which excludes volatile items such as energy prices, came in at 0.3 per cent or higher, it could warrant an outsized rise - a number that was confirmed in the data released just a few hours later.
The bond market was swift to react, with the policy-sensitive US two-year Treasury yield jumping 18 basis points, while the benchmark 10-year yield rose 11 basis points towards 5 per cent.
"The market is not taking Waller's comments too seriously, but it is flirting with the idea of a 50-basis point move from the Fed in December," said National Australia Bank head of FX strategy Ray Attrill. "If the Aussie dollar is under pressure because of what other central banks - particularly the Fed - are doing, that argues that they [the RBA] may have to go again."
RBA modelling suggested that movements in the Australian dollar account for up to two-thirds of the impact of interest rate changes on inflation.
RBA assistant governor Christopher Kent noted last month that the role of exchange rates transmitting higher borrowing costs through the economy "quickly gets forgotten".
Attrill said that the weaker currency could add to the case for further tightening from the RBA, but he cautioned against overstating the latest move.
"In the scheme of things, the moves that we're seeing are small, but if the Aussie presses down closer to US65¢, the RBA will be a bit more concerned about price pressures." Attrill said with another rate increase expected from the Fed, and the RBA likely to stay on next month, it was unlikely the Australian dollar would climb back above US70¢ by the end of the year.
He also noted that the currency had been stuck in an "excruciatingly small" trading range this year - the second-narrowest year-to-date range since its float in 1983.
